what: The Problem with Traditional Bibliometric Approaches
title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: Bibliometric analysis become cornerstone research evaluation, literature mapping, science policy. However, researchers face persistent methodological challenge: every major bibliographic database exports data proprietary schema, R packages bibliometric analysis treat one particular export format de facto universal standard. creates several practical problems: Schema lock-: Analyses built around single platform’s export format difficult extend new sources evidence emerge. Cross-database integration ad hoc: Merging records Scopus, Web Science, Dimensions, PubMed, OpenAlex typically requires custom scripts error-prone, non-reproducible, tightly coupled specific export version. Provenance gaps: records multiple origins merged flat data frame, becomes nearly impossible trace observations came source, harmonized, transformations applied. Analytical fragmentation: Descriptive statistics, network construction, comparative tests, temporal analyses often performed separate workflows lose relational structure underlying data.

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: biblioIntegrator addresses challenges introducing harmonized relational project common analytical object. Rather assuming Web Science export CSV universal shape bibliometric data, package defines small, well-documented relational schema — six core tables — can absorb records source, track provenance every transformation, serve foundation downstream analyses. vignette provides comprehensive overview package’s architecture, data model, workflow. designed read diving topic-specific vignettes (import, quality, descriptive analysis, comparative inference, networks, temporal analysis, scalable backends, Python/reporting integration).

Report: Generate reproducible outputs (tables, figures, reports). stage produces artifacts feed next, provenance table captures lineage every transformation.

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: Harmonization transforms database-specific field names formats common schema. handled automatically import functions, can also harmonize manually: harmonization step also generates primary keys (work_id, author_id, etc.) link tables together.
code: # Automatic harmonization during import scopus_harmonized <- import_scopus("scopus_export.csv", harmonize = TRUE)  # Manual harmonization (advanced) scopus_harmonized <- harmonize_import(   scopus_raw,   source = "scopus",   field_mapping = list(     title = "Title",     year = "Year",     doi = "DOI",     abstract = "Abstract"   ) )

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: Every function modifies data automatically appends rows provenance table. package uses internal mechanism: never need call function directly — called every data-modifying function package.
code: # This is an internal function, shown for illustration record_provenance <- function(proj, operation, input_ids, output_ids,                                parameters, summary) {   new_row <- data.frame(     provenance_id = generate_id(),     operation = operation,     timestamp = Sys.time(),     input_ids = paste(input_ids, collapse = ","),     output_ids = paste(output_ids, collapse = ","),     parameters = parameters,     summary = summary,     stringsAsFactors = FALSE   )   proj$provenance <- rbind(proj$provenance, new_row)   proj }

Version projects: Use semantic versioning project files track major revisions.

title: Overview and Package Architecture

code: # WRONG: Extracting and discarding the project works_df <- proj$works # ... analysis on works_df alone ...  # RIGHT: Work within the project framework describe_biblio(proj) biblio_network(proj, type = "coauthorship")

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: problem: Writing code assumes optional packages installed, leading errors systems available. ’s wrong: Different team members collaborators may different packages installed. Code fails ungracefully hard share. correct approach:
code: # Always guard optional backends if (requireNamespace("bibliometrix", quietly = TRUE)) {   # Use bibliometrix features   biblio_df <- as_bibliometrix(proj) } else {   message("Install 'bibliometrix' for extended analysis features.") }  # Or use the try_* variant biblio_df <- try_as_bibliometrix(proj) # Returns NULL with a message if bibliometrix is not available

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: problem: Treating citation counts publication patterns universal truths without acknowledging database different coverage. ’s wrong: Scopus covers journals Web Science, Web Science deeper historical coverage. PubMed comprehensive biomedical research limited engineering. OpenAlex broad varying data quality across sources. correct approach:
code: # Always report the source database when presenting results table(proj$works$database)  # Use the database column to filter or compare scopus_works <- proj$works[proj$works$database == "scopus", ] wos_works <- proj$works[proj$works$database == "wos", ]

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: problem: Aggressive name normalization (e.g., removing middle initials) careful identity resolution, leading false merges distinct authors. ’s wrong: Two authors named “J. Smith” “J. . Smith” may may person. Premature normalization collapses information needed make distinction. correct approach:
code: # Use the package's identity resolution tools proj <- resolve_authors(proj, method = "conservative")  # Review flagged cases before merging review_author_conflicts(proj)

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: problem: Combining data multiple databases without checking duplicated works appear one source. ’s wrong: Works indexed Scopus Web Science appear twice, inflating publication citation counts. correct approach:
code: # The harmonize_project function handles deduplication automatically proj <- harmonize_project(   scopus_data,   wos_data,   dedup = TRUE,   dedup_threshold = 0.85 )

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: problem: Including document types (articles, editorials, errata, letters) without filtering, leading inflated misleading counts. ’s wrong: Editorials letters peer-reviewed research articles. Including publication counts impact analyses may distort results. correct approach:
code: # Check document type distribution table(proj$works$document_type)  # Filter to articles and reviews proj_filtered <- filter_works(proj, document_type = c("article", "review"))

title: Overview and Package Architecture
text: problem: Assuming DOIs always available always unique across databases. ’s wrong: works lack DOIs (especially older publications), occasional DOI errors exist database exports. Relying solely DOIs deduplication misses matches may create false matches. correct approach:
code: # Use multiple matching criteria proj <- harmonize_project(   scopus_data,   wos_data,   match_by = c("doi", "title_year_author"),   doi_priority = TRUE )

title: Import and Harmonization
text: Bibliometric research nearly always begins data lives one place. Scopus export uses one column schema, Web Science uses another, Dimensions yet another. Even two CSV dumps service can disagree field names, delimiter conventions, encoding treatment missing values. treat export canonical shape spend time wrangling columns instead answering research questions. biblioIntegrator package takes different approach. defines common relational structure — biblio_project — provides functions normalise every incoming source structure. Import harmonization deliberately separated: Import reads raw data disk (CSV, TSV, JSON, RIS, BibTeX) API (OpenAlex, OpenCitations) produces single data frame. Harmonization (as_biblio_project()) converts data frame relational biblio_project, splitting authors, keywords references tables, normalising DOIs, logging every step provenance ledger. two-phase design means can inspect, filter repair data frame enters relational model. also means harmonization step deterministic reproducible: data frame always produce biblio_project, regardless originally created. vignette walks every supported import path, explains step harmonization pipeline , shows export results formats downstream tools (bibliometrix, Biblium, VOSviewer) expect. end able import corpus source, inspect harmonized tables, validate integrity, hand clean data analytical vignettes follow. Companion vignettes. reading one, continue v02-quality-dedup.Rmd deduplication, v03-descriptive-impact.Rmd descriptive metrics, v05-networks.Rmd co-authorship keyword networks.

text: healthy corpus shows 0 every check. Non-zero values indicate: missing_title — rows break title-based deduplication. missing_year — rows participate temporal analysis. missing_doi — rows cross-matched databases. duplicate_doi — data-entry errors un-merged duplicates. duplicate_title_year — likely duplicates even DOIs missing. negative_citations — impossible values, usually parsing error. diagnostics entry point v02-quality-dedup.Rmd.

code: validate_integrity <- function(p) {   checks <- data.frame(     check = c(       "authorship_work_orphans",       "authorship_author_orphans",       "keyword_work_orphans",       "reference_citing_orphans",       "reference_cited_orphans"     ),     n = c(       sum(!p$authorships$work_id %in% p$works$work_id),       sum(!p$authorships$author_id %in% p$authors$author_id),       sum(!p$keywords$work_id %in% p$works$work_id),       if (nrow(p$references) > 0)         sum(!p$references$citing_id %in% p$works$work_id) else 0L,       if (nrow(p$references) > 0)         sum(!p$references$cited_id %in% p$works$work_id) else 0L     ),     stringsAsFactors = FALSE   )   checks }  validate_integrity(x) #>                       check n #> 1   authorship_work_orphans 0 #> 2 authorship_author_orphans 0 #> 3      keyword_work_orphans 0 #> 4  reference_citing_orphans 0 #> 5   reference_cited_orphans 0

title: Import and Harmonization
text: biblio_project: central data structure — named list six data frames (works, authorships, authors, keywords, references, provenance) class "biblio_project". work_id: deterministic hash identifying unique bibliographic work. author_id: deterministic hash identifying unique author name string. Provenance: cumulative, append-log every operation performed biblio_project. Harmonization: process converting flat data frame relational biblio_project structure. Native format: file format (CSV, TSV, JSON) handled biblio_import() without optional dependencies. Delegated format: file format (RIS, BibTeX, etc.) handled bibliometrix::convert2df() package installed. Orphan record: row authorships, keywords references whose foreign key exist corresponding primary table. DOI normalization: process standardizing DOI strings canonical lowercase form without URL prefixes. Column resolution: case-insensitive, first-match-wins logic maps diverse source column names logical fields.

title: Import and Harmonization
text: printable checklist new users: Install biblioIntegrator: install.packages("biblioIntegrator") Load package: library(biblioIntegrator) Explore teaching corpus: example_biblio() — familiarise expected column names. Export data Scopus/WoS/Dimensions CSV (UTF-8). Inspect column names: names(your_df). Check resolution table (Section 6.1) confirm mapped. Import: x <- biblio_import("your_file.csv") x <- as_biblio_project(your_df, source = "scopus") Health check: biblio_health(x) — fix non-zero rows. Integrity check: validate_integrity(x) — verify 0 orphans. Provenance check: audit_biblio(x) — confirm source label record count look right. Export: export_biblio(x, "output_dir", "csv") archiving. Continue v02-quality-dedup.Rmd deduplication.

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: Data quality foundation valid bibliometric analysis. amount sophisticated statistical modeling, network visualization, comparative inference can compensate corpus contaminated duplicate records, missing metadata, inconsistent identifiers. vignette provides comprehensive guide diagnosing, auditing, cleaning bibliographic data using biblioIntegrator package.

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: Bibliographic databases—including Web Science, Scopus, PubMed, OpenAlex—data structures, naming conventions, quality standards. researchers export data multiple sources extended time periods, several problems emerge: Duplicate records: publication may appear multiple times due database updates, corrections, cross-database indexing Missing metadata: Critical fields titles, publication years, DOIs, author names may incomplete Inconsistent identifiers: DOIs may formatted differently (without URL prefixes), author names may vary across records Orphan records: Author-keyword-work linkages may reference non-existent records filtering issues directly impact every downstream analysis: Descriptive statistics: Duplicate records inflate publication counts, distort annual trends, misrepresent author productivity Citation metrics: Duplicate entries split citation counts, leading underestimation true impact Network analysis: Duplicate nodes create artificial connections, fragment communities, distort centrality measures Comparative inference: Unbalanced duplicates across groups introduce systematic bias hypothesis tests Temporal analysis: Duplicates different years create phantom trends

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: Quality checks precede analytical step. recommended workflow : vignette assumes already imported harmonized data using functions described vignette("v01-import-harmonize"). working raw data frame, convert first:
code: Import → Harmonize → **Quality Check** → Deduplicate → Analyze library(biblioIntegrator) x <- as_biblio_project(my_data, source = "my_export")

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: Deduplication process identifying removing duplicate records dataset. bibliometric analysis, critical duplicates inflate counts distort analyses. biblioIntegrator package implements hierarchical deduplication strategy balances precision (correctly identifying true duplicates) recall (finding actual duplicates).

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: deduplicate_biblio() function implements two-stage matching hierarchy:
code: Stage 1: DOI Matching (High Precision)     ↓ No DOI match Stage 2: Title+Year Matching (Moderate Precision)     ↓ Results combined Final: Deduplicated Corpus

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: DOI matching reliable deduplication method DOIs designed globally unique identifiers scholarly publications. Advantages: - Near-zero false positive rate - Fast computation - Handles abbreviations URL prefixes automatically Limitations: - works DOIs present correctly formatted - older publications lack DOIs - Preprints final versions may different DOIs
code:
# Demonstrate DOI normalization example_dois <- c(   "10.1000/agri.1",   "https://doi.org/10.1000/agri.2",   "doi:10.1000/ag.3",   "10.1000/agri.4",   NA,   "" )  # Show how biblioIntegrator normalizes DOIs cat("DOI normalization examples:
") #> DOI normalization examples: cat("Raw → Normalized
") #> Raw → Normalized cat("--- → ----------
") #> --- → ---------- for (doi in example_dois) {   # Simple DOI normalization (lowercase, strip prefix)   normalized <- tolower(trimws(as.character(doi)))   normalized <- sub("^https?://(dx\.)?doi\.org/", "", normalized)   normalized <- sub("^doi:\s*", "", normalized)   cat(sprintf("%s → %s
",                ifelse(is.na(doi), "NA", paste0("'", doi, "'")),               paste0("'", normalized, "'"))) } #> '10.1000/agri.1' → '10.1000/agri.1' #> 'https://doi.org/10.1000/agri.2' → '10.1000/agri.2' #> 'doi:10.1000/ag.3' → '10.1000/ag.3' #> '10.1000/agri.4' → '10.1000/agri.4' #> NA → 'NA' #> '' → ''

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: DOIs missing match, algorithm falls back title+year matching. Process: 1. Normalize titles: convert lowercase, remove non-alphanumeric characters 2. Combine year: create key normalized_title:year 3. Match combined keys Advantages: - Works publications without DOIs - Catches duplicates across databases different DOI assignments Limitations: - Higher false positive rate DOI matching - Sensitive title variations (subtitles, abbreviations, typos) - Legitimate duplicate titles exist (e.g., corrected papers, errata)

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: choice deduplication strategy involves balancing two competing objectives: Precision = (True Duplicates Found) / (Pairs Flagged Duplicates) Recall = (True Duplicates Found) / (Actual Duplicates) default doi_title_year method prioritizes precision maintaining reasonable recall using DOI matching first, falling back title+year records without DOI matches.

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: aggressive duplicate detection, fuzzy string matching can identify records similar (identical) titles. built deduplicate_biblio() : requires optional stringdist package higher false positive rate requires careful threshold tuning Results typically need manual verification However, demonstrate implement advanced users: Recommendation: Use default doi_title_year method analyses. consider fuzzy matching evidence widespread title variations prepared manually verify results.
code: if (has_stringdist) {   # Example fuzzy matching (not part of deduplicate_biblio)   library(stringdist)      # Create a small example   titles <- c(     "Cover crops and soil aggregation",     "Cover Crop Effects on Soil Aggregation",     "Machine learning for crop yield",     "Remote sensing of soybean nitrogen"   )      # Calculate pairwise string distances   dist_matrix <- stringdistmatrix(titles, titles, method = "jw")      # Find potential duplicates (distance < 0.15)   threshold <- 0.15   cat("Potential fuzzy duplicates (Jaro-Winkler < ", threshold, "):\n")   for (i in 1:(length(titles) - 1)) {     for (j in (i + 1):length(titles)) {       if (dist_matrix[i, j] < threshold) {         cat(sprintf("  [%.3f] '%s' ≈ '%s'\n",                      dist_matrix[i, j], titles[i], titles[j]))       }     }   } } #> Potential fuzzy duplicates (Jaro-Winkler <  0.15 ):

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: section documents frequent errors bibliometric data cleaning avoid .

title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: Problem: Applying deduplication raw, unharmonized data. ’s wrong: Different databases use different field names, formats, conventions. Deduplication harmonization miss duplicates look different raw form. Solution: Always harmonize first using as_biblio_project().
code:
# WRONG: Deduplicating raw data cat("WRONG approach:
") #> WRONG approach: cat("  raw_data <- read.csv('scopus_export.csv')
") #>   raw_data <- read.csv('scopus_export.csv') cat("  clean_data <- deduplicate_biblio(raw_data)  # Error!

") #>   clean_data <- deduplicate_biblio(raw_data)  # Error!  # CORRECT: Harmonize first, then deduplicate cat("CORRECT approach:
") #> CORRECT approach: cat("  raw_data <- read.csv('scopus_export.csv')
") #>   raw_data <- read.csv('scopus_export.csv') cat("  x <- as_biblio_project(raw_data, source = 'scopus')
") #>   x <- as_biblio_project(raw_data, source = 'scopus') cat("  x_clean <- deduplicate_biblio(x)
") #>   x_clean <- deduplicate_biblio(x)  # Demonstrate cat("
Practical example:
") #>  #> Practical example: raw <- example_biblio() x <- as_biblio_project(raw, source = "example") x_clean <- deduplicate_biblio(x) cat(sprintf("  Harmonized: %d records
", nrow(x$works))) #>   Harmonized: 12 records cat(sprintf("  Deduplicated: %d records
", nrow(x_clean$works))) #>   Deduplicated: 12 records

what: Mistake 2: Using Only One Deduplication Method
title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: Problem: Relying solely DOI matching title matching. ’s wrong: method different strengths: DOI matching misses duplicates without DOIs Title matching misses duplicates title variations Neither catches duplicates alone Solution: Use hierarchical doi_title_year method (default).
code:
# Show why multiple methods are needed cat("Method comparison:

") #> Method comparison:  # Create test data with different duplicate types test_data <- example_biblio() dup_doi <- test_data[1, ]  # Will match by DOI dup_title <- test_data[2, ]  # Will match by title+year dup_title$doi <- ""  # No DOI, must use title+year  combined <- rbind(test_data, dup_doi, dup_title) x_test <- as_biblio_project(combined, source = "method test")  # Show matching keys works <- x_test$works keys <- ifelse(   nzchar(works$doi),   paste0("doi:", works$doi),   paste0("ty:", tolower(gsub("[^[:alnum:]]", "", works$title)), ":", works$year) )  cat("Matching keys:
") #> Matching keys: for (i in 1:min(5, nrow(works))) {   cat(sprintf("  Record %d: %s
", i, substr(keys[i], 1, 50))) } #>   Record 1: doi:10.1000/agri.1 #>   Record 2: doi:10.1000/agri.2 #>   Record 3: doi:10.1000/agri.3 #>   Record 4: doi:10.1000/agri.4 #>   Record 5: doi:10.1000/agri.5  cat("
The doi_title_year method handles both cases automatically.
") #>  #> The doi_title_year method handles both cases automatically.

what: Mistake 3: Ignoring False Positives in Fuzzy Matching
title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: Problem: Applying aggressive fuzzy matching without manual verification. ’s wrong: Legitimate publications can similar titles: Review articles topic Sequel papers (“Part ”, “Part II”) Different papers common keywords Solution: using fuzzy matching (outside package), always verify sample.
code:
# Example of legitimate similar titles similar_titles <- c(   "Silicon and salinity tolerance in rice",   "Silicon and salinity tolerance in rice: A review",   "Silicon and salinity tolerance in rice: Response mechanisms" )  cat("Legitimate similar titles:
") #> Legitimate similar titles: for (t in similar_titles) {   cat(sprintf("  '%s'
", t)) } #>   'Silicon and salinity tolerance in rice' #>   'Silicon and salinity tolerance in rice: A review' #>   'Silicon and salinity tolerance in rice: Response mechanisms'  cat("
These are DIFFERENT publications despite similar titles.
") #>  #> These are DIFFERENT publications despite similar titles. cat("Fuzzy matching could incorrectly merge them.

") #> Fuzzy matching could incorrectly merge them. cat("Best practice:
") #> Best practice: cat("  1. Use default doi_title_year method for automatic cleaning
") #>   1. Use default doi_title_year method for automatic cleaning cat("  2. If adding fuzzy matching, require manual review
") #>   2. If adding fuzzy matching, require manual review cat("  3. Check a random sample of 5-10% of fuzzy matches
") #>   3. Check a random sample of 5-10% of fuzzy matches

what: Mistake 4: Not Recording Deduplication in Provenance
title: Data Quality and Deduplication
text: Problem: Applying deduplication without documenting changed. ’s wrong: Without provenance, analyses reproduced audited. Solution: Always check audit_biblio() deduplication.
code:
# Demonstrate proper provenance tracking x <- as_biblio_project(example_biblio(), source = "provenance demo") x <- deduplicate_biblio(x)  # Check provenance audit_log <- audit_biblio(x)  cat("Provenance after deduplication:
") #> Provenance after deduplication: print(audit_log) #>                    timestamp          operation                      details #> 1 2026-08-23 13:29:45.285139  as_biblio_project source=provenance demo; n=12 #> 2 2026-08-23 13:29:45.286178 deduplicate_biblio                    removed=0  cat("
This log records:
") #>  #> This log records: cat("  - When deduplication was performed
") #>   - When deduplication was performed cat("  - How many records were removed
") #>   - How many records were removed cat("  - The method used
") #>   - The method used  # Verify provenance has deduplication recorded has_dedup <- any(audit_log$operation == "deduplicate_biblio") cat(sprintf("
Deduplication recorded: %s
", has_dedup)) #>  #> Deduplication recorded: TRUE

text: deduplicate_biblio() uses fixed key strategy, can implement custom approaches:
code:
# Create custom deduplication keys x <- as_biblio_project(example_biblio(), source = "custom keys demo") works <- x$works  # Strategy 1: Author + Year + First Words of Title custom_key_1 <- paste(   substr(tolower(works$title), 1, 30),  # First 30 chars of title   works$year,   sep = "|" )  # Strategy 2: DOI (normalized) or Title Hash + Year custom_key_2 <- ifelse(   nzchar(works$doi),   works$doi,   paste(     substr(gsub("[^a-z]", "", tolower(works$title)), 1, 20),     works$year,     sep = "|"   ) )  cat("Custom key examples:
") #> Custom key examples: for (i in 1:min(3, nrow(works))) {   cat(sprintf("Record %d:
", i))   cat(sprintf("  Strategy 1: %s
", substr(custom_key_1[i], 1, 50)))   cat(sprintf("  Strategy 2: %s
", substr(custom_key_2[i], 1, 50))) } #> Record 1: #>   Strategy 1: silicon and salinity tolerance|2018 #>   Strategy 2: 10.1000/agri.1 #> Record 2: #>   Strategy 1: soil carbon under cover crops|2019 #>   Strategy 2: 10.1000/agri.2 #> Record 3: #>   Strategy 1: remote sensing of soybean nitr|2020 #>   Strategy 2: 10.1000/agri.3

what: Text analysis as a window into content
title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: Bibliographic databases contain rich textual information titles, abstracts, keywords. Text analysis techniques—term frequency, TF-IDF, trend analysis—reveal: Core terminology: common terms field Distinctive vocabulary: Terms characterize specific subgroups time periods Emerging themes: Topics gaining prominence recent publications

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: Use vignette need : Generate quick overview new bibliographic corpus Compute standard bibliometric metrics publication grant reports Identify cited works, authors, sources Analyze thematic patterns titles abstracts Compare impact across time periods subgroups (preliminary) Present descriptive findings publication thesis

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: describe_biblio() directly compute collaboration metrics, underlying data enable basic collaboration analysis:
code: # Average authors per document avg_authors <- nrow(x$authorships) / nrow(x$works) cat("Average authors per document:", round(avg_authors, 2), "\n") #> Average authors per document: 2  # Author frequency author_freq <- sort(table(x$authorships$author_id), decreasing = TRUE) head(author_freq) #>  #> A000008ad A00000f4d A00000f73 A0000043f A00000621 A000008c4  #>         4         4         4         3         3         3  # Map author IDs to names author_names <- x$authors$display_name[   match(names(author_freq), x$authors$author_id) ] data.frame(   author = author_names,   publications = as.integer(author_freq) ) #>      author publications #> 1   Silva A            4 #> 2 Martins B            4 #> 3 Pereira W            4 #> 4     Rao F            3 #> 5    Lima D            3 #> 6   Costa C            3 #> 7   Gomez E            3

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: h-index (Hirsch, 2005) defined : author index h h papers least h citations .
code:
# Example: understanding h-index calculation # Take an author's citation counts sorted descending example_citations <- sort(metrics$citations, decreasing = TRUE)[1] example_h <- metrics$h_index[1]  cat("Example author:", metrics$author[1], "
") #> Example author: Rao F cat("Documents:", metrics$documents[1], "
") #> Documents: 3 cat("Total citations:", metrics$citations[1], "
") #> Total citations: 61 cat("h-index:", example_h, "
") #> h-index: 3

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: Robustness: Insensitive single highly-cited paper Cumulative: increases time (decrease) Field-dependent: Varying benchmark values across disciplines Career-stage dependent: Favors senior researchers

previous_headings: 5. Author-level metrics with biblio_metrics() > Understanding h-index
title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
code: # The h-index cannot capture: # 1. A researcher with 1 paper with 1000 citations #    h-index = 1, despite high impact # # 2. A researcher with 100 papers each with 10 citations #    h-index = 10, same as someone with 10 papers with 10 citations # # 3. Different career lengths #    h-index naturally increases with time active

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: g-index (Egghe, 2006) addresses h-index limitations: author index g top g papers account least g² citations cumulatively.
code: # Compare h and g indices metrics[, c("author", "h_index", "g_index")] #>              author h_index g_index #> A0000043f     Rao F       3       3 #> A00000621    Lima D       3       3 #> A000008ad   Silva A       4       4 #> A000008c4   Costa C       3       3 #> A00000905   Gomez E       3       3 #> A00000f4d Martins B       4       4 #> A00000f73 Pereira W       4       4  # The g-index is always >= h-index all(metrics$g_index >= metrics$h_index) #> [1] TRUE

previous_headings: 5. Author-level metrics with biblio_metrics() > Understanding g-index
title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: Rewards top papers: Gives weight highly-cited works Sensitive outliers: breakthrough paper increases g h Also cumulative: increases time

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: m-index (h-index divided career length) normalizes career stage:
code: # m-index: h-index per active year metrics[, c("author", "h_index", "m_index")] #>              author h_index   m_index #> A0000043f     Rao F       3 0.7500000 #> A00000621    Lima D       3 0.6000000 #> A000008ad   Silva A       4 0.4444444 #> A000008c4   Costa C       3 0.5000000 #> A00000905   Gomez E       3 0.5000000 #> A00000f4d Martins B       4 0.6666667 #> A00000f73 Pereira W       4 0.5000000  # Interpretation: higher m-index suggests faster impact accumulation # But requires careful interpretation for very short careers

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: Citation counts simplest measure impact, require careful interpretation:
code: # Distribution of citations summary(x$works$cited_by_count) #>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.  #>    9.00   16.25   24.00   25.75   32.00   55.00  # Highly cited works head(x$works[order(-x$works$cited_by_count), c("title", "year", "cited_by_count")], 5) #>                                    title year cited_by_count #> 7            Salinity responses of wheat 2017             55 #> 1 Silicon and salinity tolerance in rice 2018             42 #> 2          Soil carbon under cover crops 2019             35 #> 4     Silicon nutrition in maize drought 2021             31 #> 3     Remote sensing of soybean nitrogen 2020             28  # Citation distribution hist(   x$works$cited_by_count,   main = "Distribution of Citation Counts",   xlab = "Citations",   ylab = "Number of Works",   col = "lightblue",   border = "white",   breaks = 10 )

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: Raw citation counts influenced : Publication year: Older papers accumulate citations Field study: Citation rates vary dramatically across disciplines Document type: Reviews receive citations original research Database coverage: databases count citing sources Language bias: English-language papers receive citations globally
code: # The problem: older papers appear more "impactful" # due to time, not necessarily quality x$works[, c("title", "year", "cited_by_count")] #>                                     title year cited_by_count #> 1  Silicon and salinity tolerance in rice 2018             42 #> 2           Soil carbon under cover crops 2019             35 #> 3      Remote sensing of soybean nitrogen 2020             28 #> 4      Silicon nutrition in maize drought 2021             31 #> 5        Cover crops and soil aggregation 2022             22 #> 6         Machine learning for crop yield 2023             18 #> 7             Salinity responses of wheat 2017             55 #> 8          Soil microbiome under rotation 2020             26 #> 9              UAV phenotyping of soybean 2024             12 #> 10        Meta-analysis of silicon stress 2025              9 #> 11       Nitrogen use efficiency in maize 2022             17 #> 12          Climate-smart soil management 2024             14

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: Normalized citations address confounding effect time field. function computes: Normalizedi=CitationsiExpectedi\text{Normalized}_i = \frac{\text{Citations}_i}{\text{Expected}_i} Expected mean citation count within chosen stratum (default: publication year).

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
code: # Compute normalized citations (by year) norm_cits <- normalized_citations(x) head(norm_cits) #>     work_id citations expected normalized #> 1 W0001f7e3        42     42.0   1.000000 #> 2 W000160f5        35     35.0   1.000000 #> 3 W0001b6e0        28     27.0   1.037037 #> 4 W0001b6e2        31     31.0   1.000000 #> 5 W0001932e        22     19.5   1.128205 #> 6 W00017da4        18     18.0   1.000000

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
code: # Values > 1: above average for the stratum # Values = 1: average # Values < 1: below average  summary(norm_cits$normalized) #>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.  #>  0.8718  0.9907  1.0000  1.0000  1.0093  1.1282  # Works above average above_avg <- subset(norm_cits, normalized > 1 & !is.na(normalized)) nrow(above_avg) #> [1] 3 above_avg #>      work_id citations expected normalized #> 3  W0001b6e0        28     27.0   1.037037 #> 5  W0001932e        22     19.5   1.128205 #> 12 W00016cdd        14     13.0   1.076923  # Works below average below_avg <- subset(norm_cits, normalized < 1 & !is.na(normalized)) nrow(below_avg) #> [1] 3

title: Descriptive Analysis and Impact Metrics
text: Figure 7. Raw vs normalized citations Figure 8. Normalized citation scores work
code: # Compare raw and normalized par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # Raw citations hist(   norm_cits$citations,   main = "Raw Citations",   xlab = "Citations",   col = "lightcoral",   border = "white",   breaks = 8 )  # Normalized citations hist(   norm_cits$normalized[!is.na(norm_cits$normalized)],   main = "Normalized Citations",   xlab = "Normalized Score",   col = "lightgreen",   border = "white",   breaks = 8 ) abline(v = 1, lty = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2) par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) # Barplot of normalized scores norm_sorted <- norm_cits[order(-norm_cits$normalized), ] norm_sorted <- norm_sorted[!is.na(norm_sorted$normalized), ]  barplot(   norm_sorted$normalized,   names.arg = paste0("W", seq_len(nrow(norm_sorted))),   main = "Normalized Citation Scores",   xlab = "Works (ranked)",   ylab = "Normalized Score",   col = ifelse(norm_sorted$normalized > 1, "darkgreen", "gray"),   border = "white",   las = 2,   cex.names = 0.6 ) abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2) text(   x = 0.5,   y = 1.05,   labels = "Average = 1",   pos = 4,   col = "red",   cex = 0.8 )

text: term_frequency() extracts counts terms titles abstracts. provides simple effective way identify common vocabulary corpus.

code: # Default stopwords are removed # You can customize them: tf_custom <- term_frequency(   x,   field = "title",   stopwords = c("and", "the", "for", "with", "under", "of", "in", "to", "a", "an") ) head(tf_custom, 10) #>           term n #> 1         soil 4 #> 2      silicon 3 #> 3        cover 2 #> 4        crops 2 #> 5        maize 2 #> 6     nitrogen 2 #> 7     salinity 2 #> 8      soybean 2 #> 9  aggregation 1 #> 10      carbon 1  # Use abstracts (if available) tf_abstract <- term_frequency(x, field = "abstract") head(tf_abstract, 10) #> [1] n #> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

code: # Identify topics with increasing frequency # Simple approach: compare recent vs earlier years recent_year <- max(x$works$year, na.rm = TRUE) earlier_year <- recent_year - 2  recent_trends <- subset(trends, year >= earlier_year) early_trends <- subset(trends, year < earlier_year)  # Frequency in recent vs earlier periods recent_freq <- tapply(recent_trends$n, recent_trends$keyword, sum) early_freq <- tapply(early_trends$n, early_trends$keyword, sum)  # Topics appearing in recent but not earlier new_topics <- setdiff(names(recent_freq), names(early_freq)) if (length(new_topics) > 0) {   cat("Emerging topics (recent only):\n")   print(recent_freq[new_topics]) } #> Emerging topics (recent only): #>    climate-smart machine learning       management    meta-analysis  #>                1                1                1                1  #>      phenotyping           stress              uav            yield  #>                1                1                1                1

what: 1.1 The Core Question of Bibliometric Enquiry
title: Comparative Inference Between Groups
text: Every bibliometric investigation eventually confronts deceptively simple question: “really distinguishes one subset publications another?” Whether comparing early-career established researchers, open-access subscription publications, domestic international collaborations, studies funded different agencies, need principled statistical framework separates meaningful patterns random noise. Without framework, reported “differences” may nothing sampling fluctuation dressed confident language.

title: Comparative Inference Between Groups
text: Rudimentary bibliometric reports frequently present descriptive statistics side--side—mean citations differ Groups B, proportion international co-authors differs, keyword frequencies differ—descriptive differences alone never sufficient. difference observed one particular sample might easily arise chance, especially number publications per group modest multiple comparisons made. Traditional parametric tests (Student’s t, classical chi-squared, one-way ANOVA) require distributional assumptions bibliometric data consistently violate: Permutation (randomization) inference sidesteps problems deriving null distribution empirically—directly data .

title: Comparative Inference Between Groups
text: Permutation inference follows directly logic design-based inference (Fisher, 1935): Null hypothesis: group labels carry information observed publication attributes. assignment labels observed data produce equally extreme statistics. Test statistic: scalar summary group–attribute relationship (chi-squared, Cramér’s V, custom statistic). Null distribution: generated recomputing statistic randomly permuting group labels. Inference: compare observed statistic null distribution.

title: Comparative Inference Between Groups
text: Permutation tests require exactly one assumption: exchangeability null hypothesis—joint distribution observations remains unchanged labels permuted. much weaker requirement normality, homoscedasticity, classical independence, making ideal bibliometric data.

what: 3.3 The Role of B (Number of Permutations)
title: Comparative Inference Between Groups
text: Convention: B = 9 999 provides good precision typical α = 0.05 testing. p close significance boundary, increase B. permutation p-value computed pperm=1+∑b=1B𝟏(χb2≥χobs2)1+B p_{\text{perm}} = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^{B}\, \mathbf{1}\!\bigl(\chi^2_b \geq \chi^2_{\text{obs}}\bigr)}{1 + B} “+1” numerator denominator ensures p-value never exactly zero bounded 1/B.

Values beyond |2| conventionally noteworthy; large values (|r| > 10) indicate overwhelmingly strong effects.

what: 8.3 Permutation Test for CA Dimension Significance
title: Comparative Inference Between Groups
code: # For each CA dimension, test whether the observed inertia # exceeds what would be expected under random group assignment set.seed(42) B <- 999 inertia_obs <- ca_result$eigenvalues[1:3] inertia_perm <- matrix(NA, nrow = B, ncol = 3)  for (b in seq_len(B)) {   perm_grps       <- grps   perm_grps$group <- sample(grps$group)   ca_perm         <- group_ca(perm_grps, variable = "DE",                                n_components = 3, min_freq = 10)   inertia_perm[b, ] <- ca_perm$eigenvalues[1:3] }  p_inertia <- numeric(3) for (k in 1:3) {   p_inertia[k] <- (1 + sum(inertia_perm[, k] >= inertia_obs[k])) /                    (1 + B) } names(p_inertia) <- paste0("Dim", 1:3) print(p_inertia)

title: Comparative Inference Between Groups
text: Tschuprow’s T similar Cramér’s V uses different normalisation accounts shape: T=χ2/N(R−1)(C−1) T = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2 / N}{\sqrt{(R-1)(C-1)}}} square tables (R = C), T = V. rectangular tables, T < V.
code: compute_tschuprow <- function(chi2, N, R, C) {   sqrt((chi2 / N) / sqrt((R - 1) * (C - 1))) }  ct <- table(grps$group, biblioData$SO_category) R <- nrow(ct) C <- ncol(ct) compute_tschuprow(cmp_result$SO_category$chi2_observed, sum(ct), R, C)

text: Cohen’s w defined w=∑∑j(pij−pi⋅pj)2pi⋅pj w = \sqrt{\sum_i \sum_j \frac{(p_{ij} - p_i \cdot p_j)^2}{p_i \cdot p_j}} pij_{ij} observed proportion cell (, j) pi_i, pj_j marginal proportions.
code: compute_cohens_w <- function(ct) {   N  <- sum(ct)   pi <- rowSums(ct) / N   pj <- colSums(ct) / N   pij <- ct / N   sqrt(sum(((outer(pi, pj) - outer(pi, pj))^2 / outer(pi, pj)) *            (ct > 0))) } # compute_cohens_w(ct)  # see ?compare_groups for built-in extraction

text: network_centrality() returns data frame four columns: degree – number neighbours (unweighted). strength – sum edge weights (weighted analogue degree). betweenness – normalised betweenness centrality, computed inverse weights stronger edges treated shorter paths. pagerank – Google PageRank score, incorporating edge weights.

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: bibliography 12 works 7 authors inevitably produce small, sparse graph. larger corpora, edge list can enormous. Thresholding — keeping edges minimum weight — primary tool controlling graph density. Setting min_weight = 1 keeps edges. Increasing threshold removes weak incidental co-occurrences, often revealing underlying structure clearly.

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: threshold increases, edges drop — isolated vertices (authors suprathreshold connections) may remain.
code: # Compare graph size at different thresholds thresholds <- 1:3 graph_sizes <- data.frame(   min_weight = thresholds,   vertices   = NA_integer_,   edges      = NA_integer_ ) for (i in seq_along(thresholds)) {   g <- bibliographic_network(x, "coauthor", min_weight = thresholds[i])   graph_sizes$vertices[i] <- igraph::vcount(g)   graph_sizes$edges[i]    <- igraph::ecount(g) } graph_sizes #>   min_weight vertices edges #> 1          1        7    10 #> 2          2        3     2 #> 3          3        0     0

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: universal answer. Guidelines: Start min_weight = 1 (default) see full network. Increase 2 3 remove noise. large corpora, threshold 3–5 common coauthorship networks. Always report threshold used.

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: Higher thresholds produce smaller, stable networks (fewer weak edges means less variability). However, also eliminate information. complementary approach build min_weight = 1 let stability analysis identify connections robust.

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: analysts prefer set threshold based distribution edge weights rather absolute value. idea keep, say, top 50% edges weight:
code: # Percentile-based thresholding g_full <- bibliographic_network(x, "coauthor", min_weight = 1) all_weights <- igraph::E(g_full)$weight  # Compute percentiles percentiles <- c(0, 25, 50, 75) pct_thresholds <- quantile(all_weights, probs = percentiles / 100)  # Resulting edge counts at each percentile pct_df <- data.frame(   percentile    = paste0(percentiles, "%"),   min_weight    = as.numeric(pct_thresholds),   edges_retained = vapply(as.numeric(pct_thresholds), function(thr) {     sum(all_weights >= thr)   }, integer(1)) ) pct_df #>   percentile min_weight edges_retained #> 1         0%          1             10 #> 2        25%          1             10 #> 3        50%          1             10 #> 4        75%          1             10

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: Beyond edge count, two useful graph metrics density (ratio actual edges possible edges) number connected components: Increasing threshold may fragment network multiple components. happens, centrality measures like betweenness (assumes paths exist node pairs) become less meaningful. Use igraph::decompose(g) extract individual components analysis.
code:
# Network density at the default threshold g1 <- bibliographic_network(x, "coauthor", min_weight = 1) cat("Density (min_weight = 1):", igraph::edge_density(g1), "
") #> Density (min_weight = 1): 0.4761905 cat("Connected components:", igraph::count_components(g1), "

") #> Connected components: 1  # At a higher threshold g2 <- bibliographic_network(x, "coauthor", min_weight = 2) cat("Density (min_weight = 2):", igraph::edge_density(g2), "
") #> Density (min_weight = 2): 0.6666667 cat("Connected components:", igraph::count_components(g2), "
") #> Connected components: 1 # Analyse individual components (if graph fragments) components <- igraph::decompose(g2) cat("Number of components:", length(components), "
") #> Number of components: 1 for (i in seq_along(components)) {   cat(sprintf("  Component %d: %d vertices, %d edges
",               i,               igraph::vcount(components[[i]]),               igraph::ecount(components[[i]]))) } #>   Component 1: 3 vertices, 2 edges

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: useful technique scale node sizes colours centrality values, making important nodes visually prominent:
code: library(igraph)  g  <- bibliographic_network(x, "coauthor") cent <- network_centrality(g)  # Map centrality to visual properties auth_map <- setNames(x$authors$display_name, x$authors$author_id) igraph::V(g)$label <- auth_map[igraph::V(g)$name]  # Size by PageRank (scaled) pr_scaled <- (cent$pagerank - min(cent$pagerank)) /   (max(cent$pagerank) - min(cent$pagerank) + 1e-10) igraph::V(g)$size <- 8 + 20 * pr_scaled  # Colour by betweenness (gradient: light grey to red) bet_scaled <- (cent$betweenness - min(cent$betweenness)) /   (max(cent$betweenness) - min(cent$betweenness) + 1e-10) igraph::V(g)$color <- rgb(0.9 - 0.6 * bet_scaled,                   0.6 * (1 - bet_scaled),                   0.6 * (1 - bet_scaled))  # Edge width by weight E(g)$width <- 0.5 + E(g)$weight  set.seed(42) plot(g, main = "Node size = PageRank, colour = betweenness")

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: defined groups (e.g., early vs. recent period), can compare network structure filtering project first:
code: # Split by period x_early <- x x_early$works <- x$works[x$works$year <= 2021, , drop = FALSE] x_early$authorships <- x$authorships[   x$authorships$work_id %in% x_early$works$work_id, , drop = FALSE ] x_early$keywords <- x$keywords[   x$keywords$work_id %in% x_early$works$work_id, , drop = FALSE ]  x_recent <- x x_recent$works <- x$works[x$works$year > 2021, , drop = FALSE] x_recent$authorships <- x$authorships[   x$authorships$work_id %in% x_recent$works$work_id, , drop = FALSE ] x_recent$keywords <- x$keywords[   x$keywords$work_id %in% x_recent$works$work_id, , drop = FALSE ]  # Compare network structure g_early  <- bibliographic_network(x_early, "coauthor") g_recent <- bibliographic_network(x_recent, "coauthor")  data.frame(   period  = c("early (<=2021)", "recent (>2021)"),   authors = c(igraph::vcount(g_early), igraph::vcount(g_recent)),   edges   = c(igraph::ecount(g_early), igraph::ecount(g_recent)) ) #>           period authors edges #> 1 early (<=2021)       7     5 #> 2 recent (>2021)       7     6

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: Beyond simply building two graphs side--side, can compute summary statistics highlight structural differences:
code: # Structural comparison compare_network_stats <- function(g1, g2, label1 = "A", label2 = "B") {   data.frame(     metric    = c("vertices", "edges", "density",                   "components", "avg_degree"),     period_A  = c(       igraph::vcount(g1),       igraph::ecount(g1),       round(igraph::edge_density(g1), 4),       igraph::count_components(g1),       round(mean(igraph::degree(g1)), 2)     ),     period_B  = c(       igraph::vcount(g2),       igraph::ecount(g2),       round(igraph::edge_density(g2), 4),       igraph::count_components(g2),       round(mean(igraph::degree(g2)), 2)     )   ) }  compare_network_stats(g_early, g_recent, "early", "recent") #>       metric period_A period_B #> 1   vertices   7.0000   7.0000 #> 2      edges   5.0000   6.0000 #> 3    density   0.2381   0.2857 #> 4 components   2.0000   1.0000 #> 5 avg_degree   1.4300   1.7100

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: biblioIntegrator builds separate networks type (coauthor, keyword, citation). Combining multi-layer network possible requires manual construction:
code: library(igraph)  g_coauthor <- bibliographic_network(x, "coauthor") g_keyword  <- bibliographic_network(x, "keyword")  # Add a type attribute to distinguish layers E(g_coauthor)$layer <- "coauthor" E(g_keyword)$layer  <- "keyword"  # Combine (disjoint union; rename to avoid clashes) igraph::V(g_keyword)$name <- paste0("kw_", igraph::V(g_keyword)$name) g_combined <- igraph::disjoint_union(g_coauthor, g_keyword)

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: Building networks different time windows comparing reveals collaboration patterns evolve. useful studying emergence new research communities.
code: # Build networks for each year years <- sort(unique(x$works$year)) year_nets <- list() for (yr in years) {   x_sub <- x   x_sub$works <- x$works[x$works$year == yr, , drop = FALSE]   x_sub$authorships <- x$authorships[     x$authorships$work_id %in% x_sub$works$work_id, , drop = FALSE   ]   x_sub$keywords <- x$keywords[     x$keywords$work_id %in% x_sub$works$work_id, , drop = FALSE   ]   g_sub <- tryCatch(     bibliographic_network(x_sub, "coauthor"),     error = function(e) NULL   )   if (!is.null(g_sub) && igraph::vcount(g_sub) > 0) {     year_nets[[as.character(yr)]] <- g_sub   } }  # Summary per year data.frame(   year    = names(year_nets),   authors = vapply(year_nets, function(g) as.integer(igraph::vcount(g)), integer(1)),   edges   = vapply(year_nets, function(g) as.integer(igraph::ecount(g)), integer(1)) ) #>      year authors edges #> 2017 2017       2     1 #> 2018 2018       2     1 #> 2019 2019       2     1 #> 2020 2020       4     2 #> 2021 2021       2     1 #> 2022 2022       4     2 #> 2023 2023       2     1 #> 2024 2024       4     2 #> 2025 2025       2     1

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: Sometimes want transform weights computing centrality — e.g., taking log weights reduce skew. igraph object allows set edge attributes directly:
code: library(igraph)  g <- bibliographic_network(x, "coauthor") E(g)$log_weight <- log1p(E(g)$weight)  # Betweenness with log-transformed weights bc <- betweenness(g, weights = 1 / E(g)$log_weight, normalized = TRUE) data.frame(node = igraph::V(g)$name, betweenness = bc)

what: 15.5 Sensitivity of network metrics to the threshold
title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: helper function explores centrality rankings change weight threshold increases:
code: # Sensitivity analysis for thresholds threshold_sensitivity <- function(proj, type = "coauthor",                                   thresholds = 1:3) {   results <- list()   for (thr in thresholds) {     g <- bibliographic_network(proj, type, min_weight = thr)     if (igraph::vcount(g) == 0) next     cent <- network_centrality(g)     cent$threshold <- thr     results[[as.character(thr)]] <- cent   }   do.call(rbind, results) }  sens <- threshold_sensitivity(x, thresholds = 1:3) head(sens, 12) #>                  node degree strength betweenness  pagerank threshold #> 1.A000008c4 A000008c4      3        3  0.03333333 0.1290688         1 #> 1.A00000905 A00000905      2        3  0.12222222 0.1267212         1 #> 1.A00000f4d A00000f4d      4        4  0.12222222 0.1648773         1 #> 1.A00000f73 A00000f73      3        4  0.27777778 0.1612960         1 #> 1.A00000621 A00000621      3        3  0.05555556 0.1273099         1 #> 1.A000008ad A000008ad      2        4  0.20000000 0.1617880         1 #> 1.A0000043f A0000043f      3        3  0.12222222 0.1289388         1 #> 2.A00000905 A00000905      1        2  0.00000000 0.2567568         2 #> 2.A00000f73 A00000f73      1        2  0.00000000 0.2567568         2 #> 2.A000008ad A000008ad      2        4  1.00000000 0.4864865         2

title: Bibliographic Networks and Stability
text: Beyond individual node metrics, whole-network statistics describe overall structure. returned directly igraph: metrics characterise network whole: Density ranges 0 (edges) 1 (possible edges). Bibliographic networks typically sparse (density < 0.3). Diameter longest shortest path. Small diameters suggest “small world” structure. Transitivity (global clustering coefficient) measures tendency triads close — high transitivity hallmark collaboration networks.
code: # Global network statistics g <- bibliographic_network(x, "coauthor", min_weight = 1)  global_stats <- data.frame(   metric = c(     "vertices", "edges", "density", "diameter",     "avg_path_length", "transitivity", "components"   ),   value  = c(     igraph::vcount(g),     igraph::ecount(g),     round(igraph::edge_density(g), 4),     igraph::diameter(g, directed = FALSE),     round(igraph::average.path.length(g, directed = FALSE), 3),     round(igraph::transitivity(g, type = "global"), 4),     igraph::count_components(g)   ) ) #> Warning: `average.path.length()` was deprecated in igraph 2.0.0. #> ℹ Please use `mean_distance()` instead. #> This warning is displayed once per session. #> Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was #> generated. global_stats #>            metric   value #> 1        vertices  7.0000 #> 2           edges 10.0000 #> 3         density  0.4762 #> 4        diameter  4.0000 #> 5 avg_path_length  1.9520 #> 6    transitivity  0.4500 #> 7      components  1.0000

Community algorithm: Louvain, Walktrap, label propagation, etc. Stability assessment: number subsamples (B), fraction, seed. Corpus metadata: number works, time span, source database(s). title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
text: Bibliometric data contains rich temporal textual signals go far beyond citation counts h-indices. Understanding research emerges topics addresses provides deeper view scientific evolution. Temporal analysis reveals growth trajectories, citation dynamics, historically seminal moments. Examining publication patterns time allows researchers identify inflection points—moments field expanded rapidly, plateaued, declined. Citation velocity shows whether research impact arrives immediately accumulates slowly across decades. Textual analysis complements temporal data revealing studied. Term frequency TF-IDF analysis extract meaningful themes titles abstracts. Trending topic detection identifies emerging research fronts become saturated. Together, methods help answer fundamental questions: research field accelerate? Growth curves reveal inflection points research attention intensified. quickly papers cited? Citation velocity distinguishes fast-moving fields slower maturation. years seminal? Reference Publication Year Spectroscopy (RPYS) identifies years exerted disproportionate historical influence. topics trending? Text analysis reveals emerging themes declining interests. research disruptive consolidating? Disruption indices quantify whether work opens new directions consolidates existing ones. vignette demonstrates combine temporal textual analyses using biblioIntegrator package.

title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
code: # Summary statistics summary(velocity$velocity)  # Classify velocity velocity <- velocity %>%   mutate(     velocity_class = case_when(       velocity >= 20 ~ "Very high",       velocity >= 10 ~ "High",       velocity >= 5  ~ "Medium",       velocity >= 1  ~ "Low",       TRUE           ~ "Minimal"     )   )  velocity %>%   count(velocity_class) %>%   arrange(desc(n)) %>%   mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))

title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
code: # Normalize velocity by field to enable cross-field comparison velocity_norm <- velocity %>%   group_by(field) %>%   mutate(     velocity_z = (velocity - mean(velocity, na.rm = TRUE)) /                   sd(velocity, na.rm = TRUE),     velocity_pct = percent_rank(velocity)   ) %>%   ungroup()  # Top 1% papers by normalized velocity top_velocity <- velocity_norm %>%   filter(velocity_pct >= 0.99) %>%   arrange(desc(velocity_z))  cat("Top 1% papers by normalized citation velocity:\n") print(head(top_velocity, 10))

title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
text: Citation trajectories model individual papers accumulate citations life cycle. Different patterns possible: Immediate impact: High initial citations, declining time Slow burn: Gradual increase, peak 5-10 years Sleeping beauty: Low initial impact, sudden late recognition Plateau: Rapid rise followed stable citation rate

title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
code: # Model citation trajectories bp <- as_biblio_project(example_biblio()) trajectories <- citation_trajectory(bp)  head(trajectories, 10) # Returns per-document trajectory parameters including peak year, # curvature, and half-life estimates

title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
code: # Classify papers by trajectory type trajectories <- trajectories %>%   mutate(     trajectory_type = case_when(       peak_year <= pub_year + 2           ~ "Immediate impact",       peak_year <= pub_year + 5           ~ "Early peak",       peak_year <= pub_year + 10          ~ "Mid-career peak",       is.na(peak_year)                    ~ "Still rising",       TRUE                                ~ "Late bloomer"     )   )  # Summary by type trajectory_dist <- trajectories %>%   count(trajectory_type) %>%   arrange(desc(n))  print(trajectory_dist)

title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
text: “sleeping beauty” paper receives little attention initially gains recognition years later. Detection criteria: Low citation rate first 3-5 years publication Sudden increase citations dormancy period Final citation count substantially field average
code: # Detect potential sleeping beauties sleeping_beauties <- trajectories %>%   filter(     trajectory_type == "Late bloomer",     total_citations > quantile(total_citations, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE)   ) %>%   arrange(desc(total_citations))  cat("Potential Sleeping Beauties:\n") print(head(sleeping_beauties, 10))

title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
code: # Plot trajectories for selected papers # Select top papers from different trajectory types selected <- trajectories %>%   group_by(trajectory_type) %>%   slice_max(total_citations, n = 3) %>%   ungroup()  ggplot(selected, aes(x = years_since_pub, y = cumulative_citations,                       group = document_id, color = trajectory_type)) +   geom_line(size = 1) +   geom_point(size = 2) +   facet_wrap(~trajectory_type, scales = "free_y") +   labs(     title = "Citation Trajectories by Type",     x = "Years Since Publication",     y = "Cumulative Citations"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +   theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Temporal and Textual Analysis
text: RPYS several limitations consider: Database coverage bias: corpus Scopus, references old works (pre-1970) may underrepresented Self-citation inflation: Fields heavy self-citation may show self-referential peaks Language bias: English-language databases underrepresent work published languages Parsing errors: Reference string parsing imperfect; years may extracted incorrectly
code: # Check for parsing issues in reference years biblio_df %>%   filter(!is.na(CR)) %>%   mutate(     n_refs = stringi::stri_count_fixed(CR, ";") + 1,     has_refs = nchar(CR) > 0   ) %>%   summarise(     total_papers = n(),     papers_with_refs = sum(has_refs),     mean_refs = mean(n_refs[has_refs]),     median_refs = median(n_refs[has_refs])   )  # Flag potential parsing issues # Very old years might be parsing errors # Very recent years (future) are definitely errors rpys_result %>%   filter(ref_year < 1900 | ref_year > as.integer(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y"))) %>%   arrange(ref_year)

code: # Co-occurrence analysis of author keywords if (requireNamespace("tidytext", quietly = TRUE)) {   keyword_pairs <- biblio_df %>%     filter(!is.na(DE)) %>%     mutate(keywords = strsplit(DE, ";\\s*")) %>%     unnest(keywords) %>%     mutate(keywords = tolower(trimws(keywords))) %>%     filter(nchar(keywords) > 2) %>%     # Create all keyword pairs within each document     group_by(document_id) %>%     summarise(       pairs = if(n() > 1) list(combn(keywords, 2, simplify = FALSE)) else list(NULL),       .groups = "drop"     ) %>%     unnest(pairs) %>%     filter(!sapply(pairs, is.null)) %>%     mutate(       kw1 = sapply(pairs, function(x) sort(x)[1]),       kw2 = sapply(pairs, function(x) sort(x)[2])     ) %>%     count(kw1, kw2, sort = TRUE) %>%     head(20)      cat("Top Keyword Pairs:\n")   print(keyword_pairs) }

code: # Compute annual growth rates for top trends if (requireNamespace("tidytext", quietly = TRUE)) {   topic_growth <- biblio_df %>%     filter(!is.na(PY), !is.na(TI)) %>%     unnest_tokens(word, TI) %>%     filter(word %in% head(trends$topic, 10)) %>%     count(PY, word, name = "frequency") %>%     group_by(word) %>%     arrange(PY) %>%     mutate(       growth_rate = (frequency - lag(frequency)) / lag(frequency),       cumulative = cumsum(frequency)     ) %>%     ungroup()      # Summarize growth patterns   growth_summary <- topic_growth %>%     group_by(word) %>%     summarise(       total_mentions = sum(frequency, na.rm = TRUE),       mean_growth = mean(growth_rate, na.rm = TRUE),       recent_growth = mean(growth_rate[PY >= 2018], na.rm = TRUE),       .groups = "drop"     ) %>%     arrange(desc(recent_growth))      cat("Topic Growth Summary:\n")   print(growth_summary) }

code: # How do term usages evolve across time periods? if (requireNamespace("tidytext", quietly = TRUE)) {   library(tidytext)      biblio_periods <- biblio_df %>%     mutate(       period = cut(PY,                    breaks = c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2025),                    labels = c("1990s", "2000s", "2010s", "2020s"),                    include.lowest = TRUE)     ) %>%     filter(!is.na(period))      period_tf <- biblio_periods %>%     unnest_tokens(word, TI) %>%     anti_join(stop_words) %>%     count(period, word) %>%     group_by(period) %>%     mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) %>%     ungroup()      # Track key terms across decades   key_terms <- c("climate", "model", "system", "analysis", "water")   evolution <- period_tf %>%     filter(word %in% key_terms)      ggplot(evolution, aes(x = period, y = proportion, fill = word)) +     geom_col(position = "dodge") +     labs(title = "Evolution of Key Terms Across Decades",          x = "Decade", y = "Proportion of Titles",          fill = "Term") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +     scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") }

text: Unlike frameworks, biblioIntegrator supports overlapping groups—work can belong one group. work multiple group labels, compare_groups() permutes complete membership rows rather individual labels, preserving overlap pattern.

title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: compare_groups() runs permutation tests assess whether two groups differ numeric variable (citations, collaboration index, keyword count, etc.). Output includes: Group-level summaries (means, medians, sample sizes). Observed test statistic (Kruskal-Wallis H ANOVA F). Permutation p-value. Bootstrap confidence intervals group differences. Effect size. permutation p-value 0.05 means observed difference unlikely arise chance random re-labelling.
code: cg <- compare_groups(   proj,   period       = c(earlier = 2000:2021, recent = 2022:2030),   permutations = 9999,   bootstrap    = 499,   seed         = 42 )  print(cg) g <- ifelse(proj$works$year < 2022, "earlier", "recent") cg <- compare_groups(   proj,   g,   permutations = 999,   bootstrap    = 99,   seed         = 42 ) print(cg) #> <biblio_group_comparison> native engine #> Chi-square: 21.29  p: 0.867  V: 0.816

title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: Mistake: Import data Scopus WoS proceed directly analysis. fails: paper appears multiple times, inflating publication citation counts. Fix: Always call deduplicate_biblio() import. Check dedup ratio—typically 15–30% records multi-database corpus duplicates.

title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: Mistake: Discard provenance table “simplify” object. fails: lose ability trace observations back source files, making analysis non-reproducible. Fix: Preserve provenance every export storage operation. biblioIntegrator automatically; manual data manipulation may break link.

previous_headings: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: Mistake: Set min_size = 1 pass vector group labels groups size 1. fails: Groups size 1 zero within-group variance, making comparison meaningless. Fix: Check table(proj$works$group) calling compare_groups(). Use sensitivity_analysis() threshold values 1, 2, 3, 5 see whether finding robust.

previous_headings: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: Mistake: Interpret high-degree nodes “important” without considering confounders. fails: Degree centrality confounded publication volume. prolific author popular keyword always high degree. Fix: Use multiple centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, eigenvector) normalise appropriately. Always consult substantive literature making interpretive claims.

previous_headings: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: Mistake: Report p-value single run fixed seed. fails: p-values near threshold (0.04–0.06) can flip different seeds different numbers permutations. Fix: Use sensitivity_analysis() report range p-values across seeds thresholds. Focus effect sizes confidence intervals, just p-value.

previous_headings: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: Mistake: Assume Arrow, DuckDB, Biblium installed. fails: Calls backend_status() biblium_backend_status() may return FALSE, breaking pipeline. Fix: Check availability early backend_status() use requireNamespace() guards.

previous_headings: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
what: 14.7 Comparing corpora of wildly different sizes
title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: Mistake: Compare 50-paper corpus 5000-paper corpus raw counts. fails: Raw counts dominated larger corpus. Fix: Normalise metrics (citations per paper, proportions) use effect sizes rather raw p-values. Report sample sizes alongside every summary statistic.

previous_headings: 14. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

text: Mistake: Estimate h-index, perform network community detection, run temporal models corpus 15 papers. fails: Small sample sizes lead unstable estimates spurious patterns. h-index 15 papers 15. Community detection 15-node graph partitions trivially. Fix: corpora 50 papers, limit analysis descriptive statistics simple visualization. Reserve advanced methods larger datasets.

title: From Data Import to Advanced Bibliometric Workflows
text: Q1: Can use biblioIntegrator systematic reviews following PRISMA? : BiblioIntegrator replace PRISMA-specific tools (screening, data extraction). However, included studies bibliographic format (CSV, RIS, BibTeX), biblioIntegrator can handle deduplication, descriptive analysis, network mapping, group comparison. screening extraction, use tools like ASReview, Rayyan, Covidence importing. Q2: combine data Scopus, WoS, PubMed? : Export database native format (CSV Scopus, RIS WoS, NBib PubMed) pass files biblio_import(). function auto-detects formats reconciles schemas. run deduplicate_biblio() merge matching records. Q3: minimum corpus size meaningful bibliometric analysis? : universal minimum, : Descriptive statistics: 20+ works (50+ better). Group comparison: 5+ works per group. Network construction: 30+ edges (community detection). Growth modelling: 5+ years least 5 works per year. thresholds, results unstable interpreted caution. Q4: Can update project incrementally new data arrives? : Yes. Import new data merging, provenance table record every new import. Use biblio_store() expansion persist updated state. run biblio_health() verify consistency. Q5: biblioIntegrator handle non-English literature? : package language-agnostic operations—schema supports titles keywords character set (UTF-8). TF-IDF term frequency analyses work language; stop-word lists English default user can specify custom lists. Q6: handle missing citation data? : Missing citations (times_cited = NA) handled gracefully biblio_metrics() normalized_citations(). Works missing citation data excluded citation-based analyses retained others. Report proportion works missing citations methods section. Q7: Can use biblioIntegrator data Google Scholar? : Google Scholar provide standard export format. Tools like Publish Perish (Harzing) export Scholar data CSV RIS. Import file biblioIntegrator usual. aware Google Scholar citation counts typically higher Scopus/WoS counts due broader source coverage. Q8: difference biblio_store() “arrow” “duckdb” formats? : Arrow (Parquet) stores data columnar files disk—optimized fast read-dominated workflows zero-copy inter-process communication. DuckDB stores data embedded relational database—optimized SQL queries incremental updates. Use Arrow data fits memory want fast columnar access. Use DuckDB need SQL queries, corpus large memory, want query without loading everything R. Q9: report permutation test results journal submission? : Always report: test statistic observed. number permutations performed (e.g., 9999). permutation p-value. random seed used. effect size bootstrap confidence interval. Example reporting sentence: “Groups differed significantly median citation count (Hobs=12.3H_{obs} = 12.3, permutation p=0.008p = 0.008, 9999 permutations, seed = 42, η2=0.15\eta^2 = 0.15, bootstrap 95% CI [0.08, 0.24]).” Q10: cite biblioIntegrator? : Use following format: Pereira, W.E. & Martinez, M.H.P. (2026). biblioIntegrator: Harmonized, Comparative Network-Based Bibliometric Analysis. R package version 0.3.0. https://github.com/user/biblioIntegrator

what: The Challenge of Large Bibliographic Datasets
title: Scalable Storage and Query Backends
text: Modern bibliometric analysis often involves datasets hundreds thousands even millions records. Source files Scopus, Web Science, OpenAlex, databases can easily reach gigabytes size. Loading datasets entirely R’s memory becomes impractical, traditional data frames scale meet demands large-scale research projects. Researchers face several structural challenges: Memory limitations: R stores data frames RAM, bibliographic datasets often exceed available memory Query complexity: Simple subsetting operations become slow datasets grow large Reproducibility: Sharing large intermediate datasets cumbersome without efficient storage formats Collaboration: Multiple researchers need query dataset without duplicating storage

")   for (table_name in c("works", "authors", "authorships", "keywords", "references")) {     arrow_rows <- nrow(x_arrow[[table_name]])     duckdb_rows <- nrow(x_duckdb[[table_name]])     original_rows <- nrow(x[[table_name]])     match <- arrow_rows == duckdb_rows && duckdb_rows == original_rows     cat(sprintf("  %s: %s (%d rows)
",                 table_name,                 ifelse(match, "✓", "✗ MISMATCH"),                 original_rows))   } }

code: benchmark_backends <- function(x, n_reps = 3) {   results <- data.frame(     operation = character(),     backend = character(),     time_seconds = numeric(),     stringsAsFactors = FALSE   )    arrow_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "bench_arrow")   duckdb_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "bench.duckdb")    # Setup   biblio_store(x, arrow_dir, "arrow")   biblio_store(x, duckdb_file, "duckdb")    # Benchmark 1: Store operation   for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) {     t1 <- system.time(biblio_store(x, tempfile(), "arrow"))     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(operation = "store", backend = "arrow",                                          time_seconds = t1["elapsed"]))      t2 <- system.time(biblio_store(x, tempfile(fileext = ".duckdb"), "duckdb"))     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(operation = "store", backend = "duckdb",                                          time_seconds = t2["elapsed"]))   }    # Benchmark 2: Load operation   for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) {     t1 <- system.time(biblio_load(arrow_dir, "arrow"))     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(operation = "load", backend = "arrow",                                          time_seconds = t1["elapsed"]))      t2 <- system.time(biblio_load(duckdb_file, "duckdb"))     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(operation = "load", backend = "duckdb",                                          time_seconds = t2["elapsed"]))   }    # Benchmark 3: Simple query   for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) {     t1 <- system.time({       works <- arrow::read_parquet(file.path(arrow_dir, "works.parquet"))       table(works$year)     })     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(operation = "query_simple", backend = "arrow",                                          time_seconds = t1["elapsed"]))      t2 <- system.time(biblio_query(duckdb_file,       "SELECT year, COUNT(*) FROM works GROUP BY year"))     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(operation = "query_simple", backend = "duckdb",                                          time_seconds = t2["elapsed"]))   }    # Calculate averages   aggregate(time_seconds ~ operation + backend, data = results, FUN = mean) }  # Run benchmark (requires both backends) if (requireNamespace("arrow", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("duckdb", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("DBI", quietly = TRUE)) {   bench_results <- benchmark_backends(x)   print(bench_results) }

title: Scalable Storage and Query Backends

code: # NULL comparison doesn't work as expected biblio_query("biblio.duckdb",   "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM works WHERE journal != 'Unknown'") # This excludes rows where journal IS NULL # Explicitly handle NULLs biblio_query("biblio.duckdb",   "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM works    WHERE journal IS NOT NULL AND journal != 'Unknown'")  # Or use COALESCE for default values biblio_query("biblio.duckdb",   "SELECT COALESCE(journal, 'No Journal') AS journal, COUNT(*)    FROM works    GROUP BY journal")

title: Python Integration, Reports and Interactive Use
text: practical workflow runs engines whenever group comparison performed logs warning disagree:
code: safe_validate <- function(x, g, tol = 0.001, ...) {   if (!isTRUE(biblium_backend_status()$available)) {     message("Biblium unavailable; running native only.")     return(compare_groups(x, g, ...))   }   vb <- validate_biblium(x, g, ...)   diffs <- abs(vb$comparison$difference)   if (any(diffs > tol, na.rm = TRUE)) {     warning("Engine disagreement detected:\n",             paste(capture.output(print(vb$comparison)),                   collapse = "\n"))   }   vb$native }

title: Python Integration, Reports and Interactive Use
text: Wrong pattern: Correct pattern:
code: biblium_compare_groups(x, g,                        permutations = 199,                        seed = 42) # Error: Biblium 2.16 backend is unavailable or not importable. st <- python_backend_status() if (isTRUE(st$available)) {   biblium_compare_groups(x, g,                          permutations = 199,                          seed = 42) } else {   message("Biblium not available; using native engine.")   compare_groups(x, g,                  permutations = 199,                  seed = 42,                  engine = "native") }

what: Mistake 7: Using biblio_report() Without Version Control
title: Python Integration, Reports and Interactive Use
text: Reports overwrite files silently. scripted pipeline, always uniquely name output files:
code: # Wrong: # biblio_report(x, "report.md") # biblio_report(x2, "report.md")  # overwrites!  # Right: date_tag <- format(Sys.Date(), "%Y-%m-%d") f <- paste0("report-", date_tag, ".md") biblio_report(x, f, title = paste("Report", date_tag))

title: LLM-Powered Bibliometric Analysis
text: Traditional bibliometric analysis served research community well decades. Keyword counting, citation analysis, co-authorship networks, h-index calculations remain indispensable tools. Yet approaches share fundamental limitation: operate surface text — words authors chose, references cited, metadata databases preserved. lies beneath surface often interesting: Semantic nuance: Two abstracts may share keywords yet address underlying research question different disciplinary angles. Implicit context: citation methods section carries different meaning one literature review, yet count equally traditional co-citation analysis. Research gaps: Gaps defined absent keyword list present — absent — conceptual landscape. Thematic coherence: cluster works may thematically unified ideas single keyword captures. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer fundamentally different lens. Rather counting tokens, build distributed representations meaning — vector embeddings capture semantic relationships texts. single LLM call can read abstract produce 768- 1536-dimensional vector encodes just words appear text means. capability opens entirely new analytical avenues bibliometric research: Semantic search: Find works address concept even use different terminology. Topic discovery: Identify latent research themes without predefined keyword taxonomies. Intelligent summarization: Generate executive summaries, methodology critiques, gap analyses hundreds abstracts seconds. Research gap analysis: Detect -explored intersections themes, methods, populations. Query expansion: Transform narrow search string comprehensive boolean query systematic reviews. Thematic classification: Assign works categories — user-defined emergent — confidence scores. Citation context analysis: Determine whether citation supports, contrasts, merely acknowledges prior work.

title: LLM-Powered Bibliometric Analysis
text: Traditional keyword search works lexical matching — query terms must appear (usually substrings) target text. two well-known limitations: Vocabulary mismatch: “climate change” won’t match “global warming” keyword search. concept ranking: document mentions query term passing treated one addresses concept throughout. Semantic search addresses problems. Instead matching words, compares vector representations (embeddings) meaning. process works follows: work’s title abstract encoded high-dimensional vector LLM. search query encoded vector space. Relevance measured cosine similarity vectors. Results ranked semantic closeness, keyword overlap. embeddings capture synonymy (“climate change” ≈ “global warming”), hypernymy (“drought” related “climate”), topical relatedness (“NDVI” related “remote sensing agriculture”).
